lines.text:
Going Underground — How Metro Systems Move the Modern City

During rush hour, a subway platform fills with commuters, tourists, and the occasional busker playing guitar near the entrance. A direction sign overhead points toward the correct line, and a display board announces the next train in two minutes. The yellow line painted along the platform edge warns passengers to stand clear of the gap between the car and the platform. This daily choreography — repeated millions of times in cities worldwide — is the invisible backbone of urban life.

A metro station is designed around the flow of people. Passengers enter through the concourse, pass through a turnstile or gate by tapping a metro card, and descend via escalator or elevator to the mezzanine level before reaching the platform. Transfer signs guide passengers switching between lines. The exit signs — often colour-coded — indicate which streets or landmarks each exit leads to. CCTV cameras, emergency phones, and help points ensure security, while fire extinguishers, defibrillators, and first aid kits are positioned throughout.

The fare system varies by city but follows common principles. A single ride covers one journey; a weekly pass or monthly pass offers unlimited travel at a discounted rate. Most systems now accept contactless payment — a simple tap at the gate. Passengers can top up their metro card at a ticket machine using cash or card. The London Underground divides the city into zones, charging more for longer journeys, while systems like Seoul charge by exact distance travelled.

Inside the car, the design prioritises density and speed. Rows of seats line the sides, with poles and handrails for standing passengers. A line map above the doors shows every stop, and a speaker announces the next station. Emergency brakes and connecting doors between cars provide safety features. The doors open automatically at each stop, and a recorded gap warning reminds passengers to 'mind the gap' between the car and the platform edge.

The London Underground — opened in 1863 — was the world's first metro system. Today, over 180 cities operate metro networks. The busiest — Tokyo, Beijing, Shanghai, Moscow — carry billions of passengers annually. Tunnels stretch for hundreds of kilometres beneath streets, rivers, and buildings, with tracks carrying trains at intervals as short as 90 seconds during peak times.

Safety underground requires constant vigilance. Guards and conductors monitor platforms. Evacuation signs mark emergency routes. The no smoking rule is universal. Barriers at platform edges — increasingly common in newer systems — prevent falls onto the track. Cleaners work through the night to prepare stations for the morning queue. Despite its complexity, the metro remains the fastest, most energy-efficient way to move large numbers of people across a dense city.

lines.text: Different cities use different names: London = 'the Tube' or 'the Underground'. Paris = 'le Métro'. New York = 'the subway'. Washington DC = 'the Metro'. Glasgow = 'the Subway'. In British English, 'subway' usually means a pedestrian underpass, not a train system — this catches many learners out.

In British English, 'subway' usually means a pedestrian underpass, not a train system — this catches many learners out.

lines.text: London's Oyster card was introduced in 2003 and revolutionised fare payment. Today, most passengers simply tap a contactless bank card. The system automatically calculates the cheapest fare — called 'fare capping'. Many world cities have similar systems: Tokyo's Suica, Hong Kong's Octopus, Istanbul's Istanbulkart.

lines.text: On London Underground escalators, there's a strict unwritten rule: stand on the right, walk on the left. Breaking this rule will earn disapproving looks and possibly verbal complaints. This convention exists in many cities but is most rigidly enforced in London. Other cities (Tokyo, Washington DC) have similar norms.

lines.text: 'Mind the gap' is one of the most recognised phrases in British English worldwide. It appears on merchandise, in films, and as a cultural reference. The original recorded announcement at some London stations used the voice of Oswald Laurence, whose widow reportedly visited the station just to hear his voice after he passed away.

lines.text: ❌ "I take the metro to go to work every day. I always go down by the escalators."
lines.name: ❌ "I take the metro to go to work every day. I always go down by the escalators."

lines.text: ✅ "I take the metro to work every day. I always go down on the escalator."
lines.name: ✅ "I take the metro to work every day. I always go down on the escalator."

lines.text: Two issues: (1) 'Take the metro to work' — no need for 'to go to'. (2) 'On the escalator' (you stand ON it, like a moving surface). 'By' = method of transport with no article: 'by metro'. But when you're physically standing on the machine: 'on the escalator', 'on the platform'.

lines.text: Non-defining relative clauses (with commas) use 'which' for things, never 'that'. 'The metro, which opened in 1863, ...' Defining clauses (no commas) can use 'that' or 'which': 'The line that/which runs north...' At B2+, this that/which distinction is a marker of grammatical precision.

lines.text: 'Be used to + -ing' = be accustomed to. The 'to' is a preposition, not an infinitive marker. 'I'm used to taking the metro.' 'I'm used to crowds.' Compare: 'I used to take the bus' (past habit, bare infinitive). Three distinct structures — used to do / be used to doing / get used to doing.
